newsitem.title: UK: COPPER PRICE HARD TO PREDICT AS VOLATILITY RETURNS.
newsitem.headline: COPPER PRICE HARD TO PREDICT AS VOLATILITY RETURNS.

text.p: After a brief period of stability on world copper markets in August, volatility returned with a vengeance in September, sending prices sharply higher then sharply lower again this week.
The price swings are the biggest in copper since Sumitomo Corp of Japan sacked its star trader, Yasuo Hamanaka, alleging he helped run up losses of $1.8 billion in unauthorized trading in copper.

And traders said the world of copper was even harder to navigate than when Hamanaka was at the helm, using a huge physical position and a blend of futures and options to help control the red metal's value.

"If Hamanaka was still trading as before, the market would be easier to read and most probably would be less volatile," said Wolfgang Becker, managing director of Iceni Commodities Brokerage in Hamburg.
"This market is ten times harder to read now than it was when Hamanaka was around," said a London Metal Exchange trader.
Three months on from Hamanaka's dismissal from Sumitomo, the market is still second guessing what Sumitomo's positions are.
While a large part of those positions will have been unwound by now, traders are convinced that they are still having some influence over the value of copper.
"It would be naive of people to think that three months on from the revelations the impact of the losses would be over," said one senior industry source.
Even more important are some big U.S. investment banks, which traders believe are the new powerhouses in copper.
This is partly because they are understood to have taken over huge positions from Sumitomo in order to help manage them.
They also have the financial clout to be able to manage these positions more effectively, traders and analysts said.
"Three months down the road it is a question now of prices being moved relatively effortlessly by just a few influential traders," said one analyst.
Options and futures traders said August's narrow trading range was largely controlled by bank participants protecting huge short option positions, possibly inherited from Sumitomo.
Three month values traded between $1,905 and $1,970 a tonne between July 30 and August 29.
But on September 2 they spiked to a 2-1/2 month peak of $2,195 before slumping back to a low of $1,915 on Friday.
The catalyst to the September spike is unclear, but the push higher did prompt heavy covering from the options market.
It would have been relatively cheap to provoke the break higher, and yet potential profits from it were large.
Some dealers said they were concerned at the amount of influence options were having on the underlying price.
Losers from recent volatility were options players short of upside cover and industry users who hedge on the LME.
"We have had a number of (trade) customers who simply do not know what to do," said one trader.
But some analysts said that recent volatility was not only the result of options or big players trading large volumes.
"I think this also reflects how close to balance the market is," Robin Bhar of brokers Brandeis said.
Despite projections of surging copper supplies in 1996 and beyond, the expected global surplus has been slower to materialise than many players had foreseen.
